Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Kwame sat in the consultation room with the measured posture of a man accustomed to analysis, yet his hands rested on his knees as if bracing for impact. At sixty-eight, he had spent decades as a policy analyst in Washington, D.C., parsing data and forecasting outcomes, but nothing in his professional life had prepared him for the sudden, violent betrayal of his own body. Three years ago, while reviewing a report at his desk, a crushing pressure had detonated in his chest, radiating down his left arm with such force that he slid from his chair before he could call for help. The heart attack had nearly killed him. He remembered the fluorescent lights of the office flickering above him as colleagues shouted, the paramedics’ hands pressing rhythmically on his sternum, the cold oxygen mask fogging his vision. What he remembered most vividly, however, was the sensation of his own heart—his own reliable, unremarkable heart—becoming a foreign agent, a traitor that had turned against him without warning. That was the moment that had never ended.

In the months following his discharge, Kwame tried to return to his routines. He went back to the office, sat at the same desk, and opened the same spreadsheets. But something fundamental had shifted. The memory of the attack did not feel like a memory at all. When it surfaced—often without any obvious trigger—it arrived with the full sensory force of the original event: the pressure in his chest, the flickering lights, the urgent voices. It was as if time had collapsed and he was once again on that cold floor. At other times, he could recall the event with clinical detachment, narrating the sequence of symptoms and interventions as though describing someone else’s medical chart, and this numbness frightened him more than the terror did. He had come to believe that he would never feel normal emotions again—that the heart attack had stolen not only his health but his capacity for genuine feeling. When his wife of forty-two years, Ama, died of cancer eighteen months after his own illness, he attended the funeral in a state of hollow composure, unable to weep, certain that the tears belonged to a man he could no longer be.

Kwame’s body had become a source of constant menace. He felt perpetually on edge, his muscles coiled, his breath shallow, as though danger lurked just beyond his peripheral vision. Even inside his own home—the same house where he had raised his children and hosted holiday dinners—he could not relax. He found himself scanning the living room for exits, checking his pulse multiple times a day, interpreting every skipped heartbeat or muscle twitch as a prelude to collapse. His body, he was certain, could no longer be trusted. It kept reacting as if the attack were still in progress, flooding him with adrenaline in response to nothing at all. He had begun to avoid physical exertion entirely, refusing to climb the stairs to his second-floor study because the slight increase in his heart rate felt indistinguishable from catastrophe.

The consequences of his avoidance had become concrete and undeniable. As a policy analyst, Kwame had been known for his sharp focus and his ability to synthesize complex data under tight deadlines. Now he struggled to hold a single train of thought for more than a few minutes. During meetings, his mind would drift to the sensation of his own heartbeat, and he would lose the thread of the discussion. His supervisor had gently suggested he take a leave of absence, and Kwame had accepted with a shame that sat in his chest like a second heart attack waiting to happen. He spent most days now in his armchair, watching the news with the volume low, his hand pressed against his sternum as if to reassure himself that the organ beneath was still beating.

What had finally driven him to seek help was not the occupational decline or the social isolation, but a single moment three weeks ago. He had been standing in his kitchen, pouring a glass of water, when his phone buzzed with a reminder for a routine checkup. The notification had been innocuous, but the sight of the word “appointment” had triggered a visceral wave of fear so overwhelming that he had dropped the glass, shattering it on the tile, and had to sit down on the floor, his back against the cabinet, waiting for his heart to stop racing. He had realized, in that moment, that he could no longer distinguish between a genuine medical threat and the mere thought of one. He was hoping, though he barely dared to articulate it, that a therapist might help him separate the two—might teach him to trust his body again, or at least to stop fearing it every moment of every day.
